analysis.one_liner: Lets the Justice Department sue to remove officeholders who engage in insurrection or rebellion.
analysis.headline: Introduced about a month after the January 6 attack, the bill drew a single cosponsor, was sent to a House Judiciary subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Attorney General sue any federal or state officeholder who engages in insurrection or rebellion, including conduct that happened before the law passed. A person found liable would be removed from office, barred from holding any federal or state office, stripped of federal retirement and survivor benefits earned through that office, and denied federal honors, commemorations, and government contracts. Congress could restore eligibility only by a two-thirds vote of each chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens whose constitutional system depends on officials honoring their oaths: the bill would give the Justice Department a clear legal tool to remove from office, and bar from future office, anyone who takes part in an insurrection or rebellion. The definition covers the President, Vice President, Members of Congress, judges, appointed officials, military members who took the oath, presidential electors, and state officeholders. Enforcement uses a clear-and-convincing evidence standard, an expedited three-judge court, and a direct appeal to the Supreme Court, so cases would move quickly. Congress could restore eligibility only by a two-thirds vote of each chamber, so removal would not be easy to undo by ordinary majorities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Citizens who rely on officials honoring their oaths

how_it_helps.text: The Attorney General could sue an officeholder who engages in insurrection or rebellion, including conduct that occurred before the bill's enactment, for removal and disqualification from federal or state office.
A disqualified officeholder would forfeit federal annuity or retirement pay and survivor benefits based on prior federal office, with a refund only of the person's own contributions.

Federal honors and commemorations would be rescinded, federal property named for the person would be renamed, and the person and entities they control at a 20 percent stake or more would be barred from federal contracts, grants, loans, and cooperative agreements.

Cases would be heard by a three-judge district court on an expedited docket with direct Supreme Court review, and the Attorney General would have to prove the violation by clear and convincing evidence.
Congress could, on petition and a two-thirds vote in each House, remove the disability and restore benefits, honors, and contracts.

analysis.who_pays: Officeholders found to have engaged in insurrection or rebellion would lose their office, their eligibility for any future federal or state office, federal retirement and survivor benefits earned from office, federal honors, and access to federal contracts through entities they control. A former president disqualified under the Fourteenth Amendment would also lose Former Presidents Act benefits.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies retroactively, reaching conduct before its enactment, which raised legal and fairness questions even among people who support penalties for insurrection.

The definition of insurrection or rebellion is broad, covering any violent act or threat of violence intended to impede a constitutional function, plus attempts, conspiracies, and incitement, and the definition of officeholder sweeps in every military member or guard member who took the oath, so the reach of a single Justice Department lawsuit would be very wide.
Survivors and beneficiaries of a disqualified officeholder would lose federal payments based on that person's service, affecting family members who took no part in the conduct.
Only the Attorney General could bring a case, so enforcement would depend entirely on the priorities of whichever administration held power, and no private citizen or state could sue.
The bill rests on a contested reading of Congress's power to enforce Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment by statute, which would likely have drawn constitutional challenges.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core aim, holding officials accountable for participating in insurrection, has strong public backing in principle, and the bill includes safeguards: a clear-and-convincing evidence standard, a three-judge court, expedited review, and a two-thirds congressional vote required to lift the penalty. But the bill's breadth is a real weakness. It reaches far beyond elected officials, applies retroactively, lets one administration decide whom to sue, and cuts off benefits to family members who did nothing wrong. A narrower version applying only to federal officials and future conduct would have carried less legal risk; as written, it was both ambitious and legally untested, which may partly explain why it attracted so little support.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee with a single cosponsor and never got a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on February 26, 2021, less than two months after the January 6 attack on the Capitol.
It was referred the same day to four committees: Judiciary, Oversight and Reform, House Administration, and Armed Services.
In April 2021 it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, which was its last recorded action.
Only one member, a House Democrat, cosponsored the bill.
The bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no companion Senate action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officeholders, including anyone who might have faced a lawsuit under the bill, are better off because it never moved: no legal mechanism now exists for the Justice Department to remove an officeholder for insurrection, strip benefits earned from office, or bar related entities from federal contracts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officeholders face no new insurrection penalty

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole sponsor.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only member to do so.

against.what_they_did: The committee never held a hearing or markup on the bill; after its April 2021 referral to the Constitution subcommittee, the bill took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor in the year and a half after introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll call exists; the bill's only support came from two House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would create the first statutory mechanism to remove and disqualify officeholders who engage in insurrection, stripping retirement benefits, honors, and contract eligibility. Officeholders' interest in avoiding that accountability runs against the public's interest in officials who honor their oaths.

industries.industry: Federal contractors tied to disqualified officials
industries.note: Any entity in which a disqualified officeholder holds a 20 percent or greater stake would be barred from federal contracts, grants, loans, and cooperative agreements, ending a channel of federal money to officials found to have attacked the constitutional order.

The bill amends the Former Presidents Act so a president disqualified under Fourteenth Amendment Section 3 loses taxpayer-funded pension and staff benefits, closing a lifetime benefit for a president who engaged in insurrection.
